title: Spreadsheets and Data with AI
subtitle: Structure it first, then let AI help you work it
summary: Practical spreadsheet work for people who keep records other people rely on: a sales log, an expense tracker, a client hours sheet. Structure the data so a formula can read it, answer questions with the handful of functions the work rests on, clean a broken export, summarise it, chart it, and use AI to write and explain formulas without ever trusting it to do the arithmetic.
description: This course is for anyone who keeps a sheet other people rely on: a sales log, an expense tracker, a client hours sheet. It does not start with formulas. It starts with the arrangement, because a total that has to read across twelve monthly tabs and past a grey TOTAL row is not a total. You will rebuild a pile of records into a table a formula can read, answer the questions a client actually asks with conditional totals and lookups that fail loudly instead of quietly, clean a broken export while keeping the proof that nothing was lost, and summarise it with a pivot and one chart that answers one written question. The last chapter draws the line that matters on a spreadsheet. Ask AI for a formula, which you can test. Never ask it for a number, because the sheet is the thing that adds and a chat reply is text shaped like a total. Every example is a Philippine record, every figure inside one is invented and labelled as invented, and anything set by rule, from a retention period to a filing deadline, is sent to the source rather than stated here. Scope note: the AI in this course's title is a general chat assistant used to draft and check formulas, not the in-app AI features now built into specific spreadsheet products. Those features change too fast for a course to describe reliably, so this course deliberately does not cover them, and points you instead at a habit, checking any AI-produced formula against rows you already know, that works whichever assistant or in-app feature you end up using. You finish able to hand somebody a figure and say exactly where it came from.
outcomes: Turn a pile of records into a table with one row per thing that happened and columns a formula can read
Answer a real question with conditional totals and a lookup, and explain where the number came from
Clean a messy export without destroying the original, and show that nothing was lost
Summarise with a pivot and build one chart that answers one written question
Get AI to write and explain formulas, then check the result before the number leaves your hands

modules.title: Data you can actually use
modules.description: Nothing later in this course works on a sheet that is a picture of a table rather than a table. One row per thing that happened, one kind of value per column, and a raw copy you never type over.

lessons.title: One row per thing that happened
lessons.content_mdx:
# One row per thing that happened

The sheet Jeric inherited looked organised, and that was the problem. Rhea sells baking supplies online from Bacolod, and she had kept her sales in one file since she started. Twelve tabs, one per month. A merged title across the top of each one. A blank row between weeks. A grey TOTAL row at the bottom of every week, and notes like "paid half, balance next week" typed into the amount column.

It was neat. It was also a printout that happened to be stored in a spreadsheet.

Jeric's first job was to answer one question from Rhea: who are our biggest customers. He could not answer it. Not because the information was missing, but because of how it was arranged.

## A table is not a printout

A printout is arranged for a human eye. Headings, spacing, a total where you want to look. A table is arranged for a machine that reads straight down a column and does not know what grey means.

The rule is short. One row per thing that happened. One kind of value per column. One header row at the top, with nothing above it and nothing that looks like it further down.

A row is one event: one sale, one expense, one block of hours worked. It carries a date, an amount, and every field you might later want to group by. That last part is the one people get wrong. If you will ever ask "how much from this customer," the customer has to be a column. If you will ever ask "how much last March," the date has to be a real date in a column, not a fact you can only recover from which tab the row happens to be sitting on.

## The three sheets this course runs on

**Sales log.** Date, reference number, customer, item, quantity, unit price, amount, payment method, status.

**Expense tracker.** Date, reference number, supplier, description, category, amount, paid from, notes.

**Client hours sheet.** Date, client, project, task, hours, billable, rate reference, invoice number.

Nine or ten columns each. Nothing clever. Notice that every one of them has somewhere for prose to live, because prose has to live somewhere, and the somewhere is never the amount column.

## What breaks a table

- A totals row sitting inside the data. When you later add up the amount column, the sheet adds every sale once, then adds the totals row too, and your year comes out roughly double. Sorting drags that grey row into the middle of March.
- Blank spacer rows put in to make it breathe. They cut the block in half as far as the sheet is concerned.
- Merged header cells, and a header spread across two rows. A column can only have one name.
- A heading repeated halfway down, so the word "Amount" turns up inside the amount column.
- Notes typed into a number column, which turns the whole column into text.
- A separate tab per month.

## Add a column, not a sheet

A tab per month feels tidy. It makes every question a twelve part job, and it makes a question about the whole year close to unanswerable. The same is true of a tab per client, a tab per platform, a file per quarter.

The general move: when you are about to create a new sheet because some records differ in one way, add a column that records that way instead. Month is already inside the date. Platform is a column. Client is a column. One sheet, more columns, and the split you wanted becomes something you ask for later rather than something you built in and cannot undo.

## What became possible

Jeric rebuilt Rhea's file into one sheet with one row per sale. He unmerged the titles, deleted the spacer rows, moved the notes out of the amount column into a notes column and a status column, and threw away every grey TOTAL row, because a total is something you compute and never something you store.

The rebuild took an afternoon and taught him nothing new about the business. Everything after it got shorter. Sales by customer became one question instead of twelve. So did sales by month, sales by item, and how much was still unpaid. When Rhea added a second selling channel later, that was one new column, not a new set of tabs.

That is the whole trade. One afternoon of restructuring buys you every question you have not thought of yet.

## Do this now

Open the messiest sheet you have. Write one sentence saying what one row of it is meant to be. If you cannot write that sentence, that is the whole job sitting in front of you.

lessons.title: Columns that behave
lessons.content_mdx:
# Columns that behave

Marilou keeps the expense tracker for her husband's aircon servicing business in Cainta. She sorted it by date to find a supplier payment, and January landed after October. Nothing was corrupt and nobody had typed anything wrong. Her dates were text that looked like dates, and text sorts alphabetically.

A column that is lying to you does not announce it. It behaves perfectly until the day you ask it to do something.

## One kind of value, one column

Every column holds one kind of thing: a date, a number, a short label, or free text. Once a column holds two kinds, every formula that touches it becomes a guess.

## Dates that are actually dates

A real date is a value your sheet understands. Text that reads 03/15/2026 is a string of characters that happens to contain digits.

Two tells. Sort the column: real dates come out in time order, text comes out in alphabetical order, which is how January lands after October. Change the display format: a real date redraws itself, text sits there exactly as typed.

Before you enter a single date into a new file, calibrate. Type a date whose day is past the twelfth, such as the twenty fifth, and look at how your tool displays it back to you. That tells you which order it is reading, which depends on the settings on that machine and that account rather than on anything universal. Then enter every date in the file the same way.

## Amounts as plain numbers

Store 1250.5. Let the cell's formatting show the peso sign, the thousands separator and the two decimal places. The symbol and the commas are how the number is displayed, not part of the number.

Type the peso sign or the comma inside the cell yourself and you risk handing the sheet a piece of text. Text will not add up, and it will not tell you it is not adding up. It just quietly sits out of every total you compute.

Decide one convention for money going out and write it down. Either every expense is stored positive and the direction lives in a separate column, or refunds and reversals are stored negative. Either works. Both in the same column does not.

## Values that only look like numbers

A mobile number, a TIN, an order reference, a barangay code: these are labels. They are made of digits and they are not quantities. Store them as text, so the leading zero on 0917 survives, and so a long reference is not quietly rewritten into scientific notation.

The test takes a second. Would adding two of these values together mean anything at all? Add two mobile numbers and you get nonsense. It is text.

## One unit per column

A cell holding "3.5 hrs" is not a number. Neither is "1h 45m". Pick one unit, put it in the header, and store the bare figure: a column headed Hours (decimal) holding 3.5 and 1.75.

Hours, rate and peso total are three columns, not one. Hours is what happened. Rate is what was agreed. The total is arithmetic, and chapter 2 is where you make that arithmetic defensible.

## Categories from a short fixed list

Free text in a category column is where an hour of your life goes. Load, Cell load, Cellphone load and Globe load are four categories to a spreadsheet and one category to you. Keep the allowed list on its own tab, keep it short enough to remember, and add to it deliberately rather than in the middle of typing.

To audit a category column you inherited, sort it and read down the distinct values. The strays sit right next to their correct twins.

## Split the combined field

A cell reading "Rhea / Bakery reels" is two facts wearing one coat. Client and project are separate columns. The rule of thumb: if you would ever want to group by only one half of it, it is two columns.

## The tells, in the order they show up

Type a number you know is a number into an empty cell and see which edge of the cell it sits against. Do the same with a word. Now you know your tool's default alignment for each. A value sitting on the text side inside a column of numbers is a text number.

The rest follow the same shape. A column that will not add. A column that adds to zero. A date column that sorts alphabetically. A leading zero that vanished. A count of the column that comes back lower than the number of rows you can see on the screen.

When you find one, fix the column, not the cell. One bad cell is almost always a habit that produced a hundred.

## Do this now

Type a number into one empty cell and a word into another, and note which edge each one sits against. Now run down the amount column of a sheet you keep and find the values sitting on the wrong side.

lessons.title: Raw, working, output
lessons.content_mdx:
# Raw, working, output

In July a client asked Jeric where one figure in the March summary had come from. He opened the file. The March sheet had been cleaned, corrected, re-sorted and added to for four months. There was no version of March as it had arrived, so there was nothing he could show her except the same number again, which is not evidence. It is the same claim repeated louder.

Nothing had been done dishonestly. The file simply had no memory.

## Three layers, one file

**Raw.** The export exactly as it arrived, or the entries exactly as first written. You never type over this. Not to fix a spelling, not to delete an obviously junk row.

**Working.** A copy of raw, where cleaning happens and formulas live. Everything you do here is done to a copy, which means everything you do here can be undone and, more to the point, compared.

**Output.** What somebody else reads: the summary, the invoice backup, the report. It is produced from working, and it holds no figure that was typed in by hand.

Chapter 3 is about the cleaning itself. The layering has to exist before the cleaning starts, because an edit made directly on raw data cannot be undone and cannot be explained. Once you have typed over the export there is no earlier truth to compare against, and "I fixed it" is not a record of anything.

Keeping the raw copy costs one tab and one minute. Not keeping it costs you the only conversation that matters.

## A short data dictionary

One tab, one line per column, saying what that column holds and in what unit. Above the lines, one sentence saying what a single row is.

For Rhea's sales log that sentence is: one row is one item sold to one customer on one date. Then the lines under it. Date is the date the order was placed, not the date it shipped. Amount is quantity times unit price, in pesos, before shipping. Status is one of Paid, Partial or Unpaid. Reference is the order number from the platform.

Ten minutes of writing. It is the difference between a sheet somebody else can pick up and a sheet that only works while you are awake and answering messages.

## Names and dates on files

Date first in the filename, year then month then day, so sales-log-raw-2026-03-31 sits next to sales-log-raw-2026-04-30 in the right order forever. Keep last month's file rather than saving over it, and never final2 or FINAL-latest. Some tools keep a version history for you, and how far back that goes is a thing to check in your own tool rather than assume.

## The reference column

Every row that carries an amount should carry the number of the document behind it: the official receipt, the invoice, the transaction reference, the platform order number. That is what lets somebody walk from the figure to the document that produced it, and it is the walk this whole course is arranged around.

## What you can still defend months later

Four tests decide whether a figure survives a challenge, and two of them are the spreadsheet's job. You can check both in a minute. The raw version still exists, untouched. Any change made since is visible, with a note saying what changed and why.

The other two are about the record rather than the file: whether it was written near the time it happened, and whether it points at a document that exists. Bookkeeping Basics for Freelancers works through all four properly and this course assumes it.

## Keeping it, and for how long

Records that support a filing have to be kept, and there is a required period. That period, the acceptable form, and whether a spreadsheet stands on its own or has to be backed by something else are real questions with real answers, and they are not this course's to state. They are set by rule, they change, and a figure taken from a lesson written at some point in the past is exactly how somebody ends up short.

Get the current answer from BIR directly, from your Revenue District Office, or from a bookkeeper who works with businesses like yours. Then do the thing hardly anyone does: write the answer on your dictionary tab, with the date you got it and who told you. In two years you will not remember, and the note will tell you both what you were told and how stale it has become.

## Do this now

Duplicate the last export somebody sent you and put the download date in the copy's name. Then write the first line of its dictionary tab: one sentence saying what a single row is.

quiz.prompt: Jeric takes over a small shop's sales file. It has twelve tabs, one per month, each with a merged title across the top, blank rows between weeks and a grey TOTAL row at the bottom of every week. The owner wants to know which customers spent the biggest amounts this year. What is the right first move?

options.text: Sort every tab by customer so each customer's rows sit together, then read the twelve blocks off the screen and total them.
Keep the twelve tabs and add a thirteenth summary tab where he types each month's TOTAL figure across by hand at the end of the month.
Rebuild it as one sheet with one row per sale, where the month is readable from a real date column and no totals sit inside the data.
Ask the owner to send the receipts again so he can start from the source documents instead of touching the file she already keeps.

quiz.explanation: The question is about the whole year and the file is built as twelve printouts, so no amount of sorting or summarising fixes it. Rebuilding to one row per sale puts the month back inside the date column, which turns month, customer, item and status into things you ask for later rather than things the file's shape decides for you. Copying totals across by hand adds a number nobody can trace back. Going back to the receipts throws away records the owner already kept.

quiz.prompt: Marilou's expense tracker runs down one long sheet, with a grey row reading TOTAL after each month's block of entries. She adds up the whole amount column to get the year, and the figure comes out at roughly twice what the business actually spent. What is happening?

options.text: The monthly TOTAL rows sit inside the amount column, so every expense is added once and then again inside a total.
The January block was pasted in below December when she built the sheet, so that month is being counted at both ends of the year.
The blank spacer rows she left between the months are being read as zeros, and a long run of zeros throws the total out.
Some amounts were typed with a peso sign in front, so they are text, and the sheet counts those rows as well as the numbers.

quiz.explanation: A total stored inside the data is just another number in the column, so any later sum adds it alongside the rows it summarises. That is where the doubling comes from, and it is why a totals row belongs outside the data or, better, nowhere at all: a total is computed, not stored. Blank rows contribute nothing to a sum. A block pasted in the wrong place is still counted once. Amounts stored as text get skipped by a sum, which makes a total too small rather than too large.

quiz.prompt: A VA pastes a customer list from a client's selling platform, where the numbers are shown in full with the leading zero, into a fresh sheet. The mobile numbers arrive as 9171234567 instead of 09171234567, and that column is used to send order updates. What should she do?

options.text: Set the column to hold text, then paste the numbers in again from the source, because a mobile number is a label and not a quantity.
Build the missing zero back on in a spare column with a formula, and use that second column whenever she sends the updates out.
Widen the column and change its number format to show eleven digits, since the leading zero is only being hidden by the display.
Leave it as it is, because anyone reading a Philippine mobile number knows a zero belongs in front and can put it back when dialling.

quiz.explanation: The zero was not hidden, it was thrown away, because the column was treated as a quantity and a leading zero carries no value in a number. The fix is at the column: tell the sheet the column is text, then bring the data in again from the source. Patching it with a formula assumes every entry is an eleven digit Philippine mobile, which breaks on a landline or a foreign number. And a phone list gets read by people in a hurry, so a known defect left in it becomes a message sent to the wrong person.

quiz.prompt: In her sales log, Rhea has typed "1200 (paid half, balance next week)" into the amount cell for one order. The sheet now refuses to add that column up at all. How should that row be recorded instead?

options.text: Keep the note inside the amount cell but colour that cell differently, so anyone reading the sheet can see the sale is not settled yet.
Split it into two rows of six hundred each, one marked paid and one marked unpaid, so the amount column matches the cash received.
Leave the amount column for notes like this one and keep a second, cleaner column beside it holding only the figures a formula reads.
Put 1200 in the amount column on its own, and carry the rest of what that cell said in a status column and a notes column, where prose lives.

quiz.explanation: One kind of value per column. The amount of the sale is 1200 whether or not all of it has been paid, so 1200 is what the amount column holds, and the payment situation becomes a status value plus a line of prose. Colouring the cell tells a formula nothing. Splitting the sale into two rows breaks one row per thing that happened and quietly turns one order into two. Keeping a dirty column and a clean column side by side gives you two versions of the truth and no way to know which one anybody used.

quiz.prompt: In July a client queries one line in the March summary Jeric sent her. He wants to show her where that figure came from rather than just repeating it. What lets him do that?

options.text: He runs the summary again from the working sheet, and if the number comes out the same he tells her it has been confirmed.
The row carries the order reference, so he opens the untouched March export, finds that row, and pulls up the document behind it.
He opens the file's version history to see who changed what during March, and sends her the earliest version of the sheet he can find.
He rebuilds March from the bank statement instead, since money that actually moved is stronger evidence than a row in a spreadsheet.

quiz.explanation: Traceability is a reference number plus a raw copy that still exists. With both, any figure walks back to the document that produced it, and that walk is what the client is actually asking for. Recomputing from the same working sheet proves only that the sheet agrees with itself. Version history varies by tool and was never designed to answer this. A bank statement shows money moving but not what it was for, so rebuilding March from it invents a second set of records to disagree with the first.

quiz.prompt: A VA downloads a CSV export from a client's selling platform, opens it, deletes two junk rows above the headers, corrects four misspelled customer names, saves over the file, and works from it all month. What was the mistake?

options.text: Nothing was lost here, since an export is produced by the platform and can be downloaded again exactly as it first came.
She should have made the same fixes but marked every changed cell in a different colour, so a later reader can see what she touched.
She should have worked on a copy and left the export untouched, so that the cleaned sheet could still be compared back against it.
She should have removed the junk rows only, since correcting a customer's name is a change that needs the client to approve it first.

quiz.explanation: Raw is the layer you never type over, and the reason is comparison rather than tidiness. With the export intact you can show that the cleaned sheet has the same row count and the same total, and that the four names are the only differences. Assuming you can download it again is a bet on somebody else's system. Colouring cells records that something changed but not what it was before. The name fixes are reasonable work; doing them on a copy is what makes them defensible.

quiz.prompt: Rhea asks Jeric how long she needs to keep the receipts and the spreadsheets behind them. "A few years, di ba?" she says, already reaching for the box under the counter. What should he tell her?

options.text: The obligation exists and the period is set by rule, so get the current answer from BIR or a bookkeeper and write it down with the date.
Keep everything indefinitely and the question never arises, since storage costs her nothing and the box is already under the counter.
She is probably close enough, so keep to the period she already has in mind and only check it if somebody ever asks.
The period applies to registered businesses only, so as an online seller she can keep whatever she personally finds useful and drop the rest.

quiz.explanation: There is a required retention period, and it is not a number to take from a course, a forum, or a confident friend, because these things change and getting it wrong is expensive in exactly the situation where you need the records. The figure in her head may be well short, and this course does not correct it with a second number, because the only one that binds her is the current one at the source. Say the obligation exists, send her to BIR, her Revenue District Office or a bookkeeper for the current figure, and write the answer, the date and the source on the dictionary tab. Guessing high is not free either, since a pile nobody can search is not a record.

quiz.prompt: Jeric goes on leave and hands the client hours sheet to a colleague. It has a column headed Rate, one headed Amt, and one headed Type holding values like S, B and NB. The colleague messages him twice on day one. What should have been in the file?

options.text: A comment on each header cell explaining what the codes in that column mean, so the note sits where the reader is already looking.
A handover message to the colleague listing what every code stands for, since it is the person who needs the explanation and not the file.
Longer column headings that spell out each code in full, so that nothing anywhere in the sheet needs explaining in a second place.
A dictionary tab carrying one line per column saying what it holds, sitting above one sentence saying what a single row represents.

quiz.explanation: A data dictionary is a tab, not a favour you do for one colleague once. One line per column, living in the file and travelling with the file, plus the sentence everything else depends on: what one row is. Cell comments are easy to miss, get stripped when a sheet is exported, and cannot say what a row means. A handover message is gone by the second week. Headings long enough to define every code make the sheet unreadable and still leave nowhere to say that Date means the date the work was done.

modules.description: A small set of functions answers the questions a sales log, an expense tracker or an hours sheet is actually asked. The skill is knowing which question you are asking, and referencing the data so the answer does not quietly break next month.

lessons.title: Totals, counts, and conditions
lessons.content_mdx:
# Totals, counts, and conditions

Jeric keeps his own client hours sheet alongside the files he manages for other people. One row is one block of work: date, client, project, task, hours, billable, rate reference, invoice number.

On the fifth of every month the same question arrives in three different shapes. How many hours did you bill us last month? How many of those were on the migration? How many separate sessions was that?

Every one of them is a total or a count with a condition hanging off it. That is the bulk of the job.

## Write the question in words first

Before you touch a formula, write the sentence you are answering. Put it in a spare cell above the working area: "Total billable hours, client LOP-01, July only."

The sentence tells you three things. What you are adding up, which is hours. What you are filtering on, which is client, month and billable. And what every row must carry for that filter to work at all.

If the sentence names something your columns do not hold, stop and fix the columns. No formula will pull a month out of a date you typed as text.

## Plain first, then the conditional forms

SUM adds a range of numbers. COUNT tells you how many cells in a range hold a number. COUNTA tells you how many are not empty, whatever is sitting in them. AVERAGE adds and divides.

On their own those four answer almost nothing, because a real question usually carries a condition: this client, this month, this category, this status. The conditional forms take the same range plus a rule.

- **One condition.** SUMIF takes the range to test, the rule, and the range to add. Total the hours column where the client column reads LOP-01.
- **Several conditions.** SUMIFS adds the same hours, but only where the client matches, the date falls on or after the first of July, and the date falls on or before the thirty first.
- **Counting instead of adding.** COUNTIF and COUNTIFS take the same rules and return how many rows matched.

Here is that July, client-LOP-01 question as an actual formula, in Google Sheets and Excel syntax, both of which take SUMIFS in the same order: the range to add first, then pairs of range-then-rule.

```
=SUMIFS(D2:D500, B2:B500, "LOP-01", A2:A500, ">="&DATE(2026,7,1), A2:A500, "<="&DATE(2026,7,31))
```

Read it left to right: add column D (Hours), where column B (Client) equals LOP-01, and column A (Date) falls between the first and last of July 2026. COUNTIFS drops the sum range and repeats the same pairs, so counting sessions instead of adding hours is the same formula with SUMIFS replaced by COUNTIFS and the leading sum range removed.

Your tool's exact syntax may differ slightly, for instance where a date has to be typed or how a locale expects arguments separated, so check its own formula reference before you rely on this shape.

One practical note. If your sheet refuses the comma between arguments, your locale is set to use semicolons. Type the separator your own tool accepts. The shape of the formula does not change.

## Counting numbers is not counting rows

Rhea's sales log came out of her selling platform as an export. COUNT on the amount column returned zero. COUNTA on the same range returned every row.

Nothing was missing. The amounts had arrived as text that looks like numbers, so there was no number in the range for COUNT to find. That column will also sum to zero, quietly, with no warning anywhere.

The gap between COUNT and COUNTA is the cheapest test you own. Run both on any column somebody handed you. If COUNT sits far below COUNTA, the column is text and nothing built on it can be trusted. Converting it is chapter three's work. Knowing before you quote a figure is this lesson's.

## A blank is not always a zero

Marilou added a delivery charge column to her expense tracker. It sits blank on the rows where she collected the parts from the supplier herself.

AVERAGE skips blanks entirely, so what it returns is the average charge across deliveries, not across purchases. Neither figure is wrong. They answer different questions, and only you know which one was asked.

Decide what a blank means in this column before you average it, and write the decision on the data dictionary tab. If blank genuinely means zero, put the zero in.

## A range that still works next month

A formula reading rows 2 to 240 is right today and wrong the moment somebody types row 241. Two ways out. Point at the whole column, so anything added underneath is included. Or turn the block into a named table, if your tool offers one, so the range grows as rows arrive. Check what yours calls that.

Whichever you use, keep the totals off the data. A total sitting inside the range gets added to itself the next time the range grows.

## Read it back as a sentence

When the formula returns something, say it aloud in words and compare it with the sentence you wrote at the start. "Add the hours column where the client is LOP-01, billable is yes, and the date is in July."

If the two sentences differ, the number is wrong even when it looks reasonable. This catches the ordinary faults: a rule pointing at the wrong column, a date range ending on the thirtieth of a thirty one day month, a client code carrying a trailing space.

## What you can now do

Take a question somebody actually asked about a sales log or an hours sheet, write it as one sentence, build the conditional total or count that answers it, and say in plain words which rows the formula counted and which it left out.

lessons.title: Lookups that do not lie
lessons.content_mdx:
# Lookups that do not lie

Jeric's hours sheet carries a rate reference on every row and no rate. The rates live on a separate tab, one row per client. To invoice, he needs each row's rate sitting beside its hours.

Typing them in by hand works. It works right until a rate changes and he misses two rows out of three hundred, and then it has been wrong for a month and nobody knows.

A lookup does the fetching: take the key on this row, find it in the reference table, bring back a value from the same row over there.

## The four things a lookup needs

Whatever your tool calls the function, you supply the same four things. The key you are looking for. Where to look for it. Which value to bring back once it is found. Whether the match has to be exact.

Some tools let you supply a fifth: what to return when nothing matches.

Function names for this differ between products, between versions of the same product, and sometimes between the desktop and the browser version, so treat the formula below as a shape to adapt rather than something to retype unchanged. Open your own tool's function list under lookup and confirm what is actually there before you commit to it.

Here is Jeric's rate lookup written out in full, in the newer function most current spreadsheet tools now offer:

```
=XLOOKUP(B2, Rates!A:A, Rates!B:B, "NO RATE", 0)
```

Read it as the four things above, in order: the key is B2, the client code on this row. Where to look is Rates!A:A, the code column on the Rates tab. What to bring back is Rates!B:B, the rate column on that same tab. "NO RATE" is what to show when nothing matches, and the trailing 0 forces an exact match rather than a nearest-below guess.

On an older copy of Excel without XLOOKUP, the same job is done with VLOOKUP, which only ever looks to columns right of its key column:

```
=VLOOKUP(B2, Rates!A:B, 2, FALSE)
```

Here the key is still B2, the table to search is Rates!A:B, 2 says bring back the second column of that range, and FALSE is what forces the exact match. VLOOKUP has no built-in "what to show when nothing matches", so it is usually wrapped in IFERROR to produce the same loud failure:

```
=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(B2, Rates!A:B, 2, FALSE), "NO RATE")
```

Your tool's exact syntax may differ slightly, for instance the order of arguments or what a missing-match placeholder is called, so check its own formula reference before you rely on either shape above.

## Match on a code, never on a name

Jeric has two clients called Santos: Ana Santos Catering in Tagum, and R. Santos Hardware in Panabo. A lookup on the surname finds the first Santos row it meets and returns that rate. Nothing about the result looks wrong. It is simply the other client's money.

Names break in ways codes cannot. A trailing space. Inc with a full stop and Inc without. Ma. and Maria. A middle initial somebody added in June.

So assign a short code once, when the client is first taken on, write it into the rate reference column at the moment each record is created, and match on that. LOP-01 either matches or it does not.

## Exact matching, and the trap next to it

Lookup functions commonly offer a second mode. Instead of the exact key, it finds the closest key below the one you asked for. It exists for banded lookups: tiers, brackets, grade bands.

Depending on the tool, that mode may be the default or may sit one argument away from it, and it expects the reference table to be sorted before it behaves at all. If you did not choose it deliberately it hands you a neighbouring row and says nothing, because a near miss and a hit look identical in the cell.

Set exact matching every time. Leave it only when you can say out loud why a band is what you want.

## A gap you can see beats a number you cannot

When there is no match, some tools return an error and some return whatever you told them to return.

Do not tell it to return zero. Zero adds silently into every total below it, and a client with no rate then leaves no mark anywhere. Blank does the same thing.

Return something loud instead. The text NO RATE cannot be summed, so it stops you at the total rather than at the invoice. Filter that column for it before anything leaves your hands. A visible gap costs five minutes. A silently wrong rate costs a conversation with a client you would rather keep.

## One row per key, and prove it

The reference table gets its own tab. One row per key, no duplicates, keys that never change once issued, no spacer rows through the middle of it.

Marilou's supplier tab brings a category across into her expense tracker. When one supplier was appearing under the wrong category, the formula was not the problem. That supplier had been entered twice, months apart, with two different categories, and the lookup was returning whichever row it reached first.

So check before you trust it. Next to the key column, count how many times each key appears in that same column, using a conditional count. Sort that helper column highest first. Anything above one is a fault to fix now, not after the invoices go out. Run the check again every time somebody adds rows to the reference tab, because that is when duplicates arrive.

## What a lookup does not solve

A lookup brings back what the reference table says today. If a client's rate changed part way through the month, every historical row quietly takes the new figure the next time the sheet recalculates.

That is the next lesson's problem, and it is the one that costs real money.

## What you can now do

Pull a rate or a category across from a reference tab using an exact match on a code you assigned, make an unmatched row announce itself instead of returning zero, and prove the reference table holds no duplicate keys before you rely on a single figure it produced.

lessons.title: Arithmetic you can defend
lessons.content_mdx:
# Arithmetic you can defend

Every figure in this lesson is invented so the arithmetic is visible. The method is the part to keep.

## Fill down, and what has to stay still

Jeric parks his rate in a spare cell off to the side of the data, K1, adds a new column I for the peso total, writes I2 as that row's hours times K1, and drags it down two hundred rows.

Row 2 is right. Every row under it reads zero.

A reference slides when a formula is copied. Dragging down turned K1 into K2, then K3, then K4, all of them empty. To hold a reference still, pin it with dollar signs. That is what $K$1 means: stay on column K, row 1, wherever this formula is copied to.

The tell is a column of zeros, or a total that looks light. The check takes ten seconds. Click the formula on the last filled row and read what it actually points at. Do that before you invoice, every time you fill a new column down.

## A rate that changes part way through

One of Jeric's clients agrees a higher rate starting the sixteenth. The tempting move is to open K1 and type the new number.

That rewrites history. Every hour logged in the first half of the month is now priced at the new rate, and the invoice he already sent no longer matches his own sheet. He cannot explain the difference, because the old figure is gone.

Two honest options. Add a rate column to the hours sheet and stamp each row with the rate that applied on the day the work happened. Or add a row to the rate tab with an effective-from date, and look up the rate that was in force on that row's date.

Either way an old row keeps its old number. The rule underneath both: never edit a cell whose previous value is printed on a document you have already sent.

## Percentages are division wearing a costume

**Share of a total.** Marilou wants each expense category as a share of the month. That is the category total divided by the grand total, with the grand total pinned so it does not slide as she fills down. In this made up month, materials of ₱42,000 against a total of ₱120,000 gives 0.35.

**Change between two periods.** This period minus last period, divided by last period. Rhea's invented July of ₱96,000 against an invented June of ₱80,000 is ₱16,000 divided by ₱80,000, or 0.20. A negative answer means down, and it should stay negative.

If last period was zero there is no percentage. It went from nothing to something. Say that in words rather than showing a figure your reader cannot interpret.

Percent formatting displays a stored 0.35 as 35 percent. It does not turn a typed 35 into a share. Type the division, not the display.

## Rounding, and where the centavos go

Three billing lines, each hours times rate, each landing with a tail past two decimal places. Round every line to centavos and add them up, and you can finish a centavo or two away from rounding the total at the end. Both are defensible. They are different numbers.

Pick one rule and hold to it: round at the point where the figure becomes money on a document, and let everything upstream carry full precision.

Know as well that formatting a cell to two decimals changes only what you see. The stored value keeps its tail and still adds the long way, which is exactly how a total ends up disagreeing with the column of numbers printed above it. If you need a value genuinely rounded, round it with a formula.

## The two checks that catch the ordinary mistakes

**Cross-foot it.** Lay the summary out with clients down the side and weeks across the top. Add a total column on the right and a total row along the bottom. Add up the row totals, then add up the column totals. They must agree. When they do not, a range has missed a row or a column, and you have found the fault in seconds instead of hearing about it from a client.

**Recompute one row by hand.** Take a row at random, not the first one, and work it out on paper. Hours times rate, minus whatever comes off, and compare. The first row is usually the one you built the formula against, so it agrees with itself and proves nothing.

Those two checks come back later in this course, unchanged, as the checks you run on a formula an AI tool wrote for you.

## What you can now do

Fill a rate calculation down a column without it sliding, keep a mid-period rate change out of figures you already sent, compute a share and a change without a formatting trick, and prove a summary adds up in both directions before anybody else sees it.

quiz.prompt: One of Jeric's clients agreed a higher hourly rate starting the sixteenth. He opened the single rate cell his whole hours sheet points at, typed the new figure, and now the first half of the month no longer matches the invoice he already sent. What should he have done instead?

options.text: Stamp every row with the rate that applied on the date that work happened, so old rows keep old figures
Adjust the first half's logged hours down until the sheet's total lands back on the invoice he sent
Round the month's total to the nearest peso, which absorbs a difference this small without any rewrite
Start a second hours sheet on the sixteenth, so that each sheet only ever holds one rate from top to bottom

quiz.explanation: Editing the rate cell rewrote history. Hours logged before the change are now priced at the new rate, and the figure on the sent invoice cannot be reproduced from the sheet. The fix is to make the rate part of the record, either as a rate column stamped per row or as a dated rate on the reference tab. A second sheet splits one month across two files and breaks every later total, and adjusting hours falsifies the record to hide the problem.

quiz.prompt: Rhea's sales log arrives as an export from her selling platform. COUNT on the amount column returns 0, COUNTA on the same range returns 240, and every row visibly shows an amount. What has she just learned about that column?

options.text: COUNT only reads a column formatted as currency, so she needs to apply peso formatting to it first
COUNT skips the header row, and this export repeated its header part way down the sheet as well
The range in her COUNT stops above the first row of data, so it is testing a block of empty cells
The amounts arrived as text, so there is no number in that range to count or to add

quiz.explanation: COUNT counts numbers. COUNTA counts anything that is not empty. A large gap between the two is the standard tell that a column of digits is text, and that column will sum to zero without warning. Formatting does not convert text into numbers, and a range pointed at the wrong rows would have driven COUNTA to zero as well.

quiz.prompt: Marilou's supplier tab holds one row per supplier and feeds a category across into her expense tracker. One supplier's expenses are coming back under the wrong category. Before she changes a single formula, what should she check first?

options.text: Whether the tracker gained more rows this month than last, which would explain a shifted result
Whether she sorted the tracker after filling the formulas down, since sorting reorders the results
Whether the category wording on the supplier tab is spelled the way her tracker's column spells it
Whether that supplier appears more than once on the supplier tab, using a count on the key column

quiz.explanation: A lookup returns the first row whose key matches, so a supplier entered twice returns whichever of the two rows it meets first, and which one that is can change when somebody sorts the tab. Counting each key against its own column and sorting the count highest first finds every duplicate in one pass. The other checks are worth doing later, but none of them explains a result that looks completely normal in the cell.

quiz.prompt: Jeric fills a formula down 200 rows. Each row should be that row's hours times the single rate held in cell K1, off to the side of the data. Row 2 is correct and every row below it reads zero. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The formula was copied rather than dragged, and copying will not carry a formula into the rows below
The reference to K1 was never pinned, so each copied row points one cell further down an empty column
The rate in K1 is formatted as currency, so the multiplication returns a value the column cannot show
The hours column below row 2 is stored as text, which multiplies out to zero on every row after it

quiz.explanation: An unpinned reference slides as the formula is copied. K1 becomes K2, then K3, and the rest of that column is empty. Pinning it as $K$1 holds it in place. Hours stored as text would raise an error or refuse to multiply rather than produce a clean run of zeros, and currency formatting only changes the display. The habit that catches this is clicking the last filled row and reading what its formula actually points at.

quiz.prompt: A client asks Jeric how many separate work sessions he logged on the migration project in July. Not the hours: the number of sessions. Which shape of formula answers exactly that question?

options.text: An average of the hours column, filtered to the migration project, times the number of days in July
A sum with conditions on the project column and on the date range, run across the hours column itself
A count with conditions on the project column and on the date range, run across the rows of the log
A count of the filled cells in the hours column, which returns every session he has logged in that sheet

quiz.explanation: One row is one session, so the question is a count of the rows matching two conditions, not a total of hours. The conditional sum answers the question he was asked last month rather than this one. Counting filled cells returns every session for every client since the sheet began, because it carries no conditions at all.

quiz.prompt: Jeric adds a new client to his hours sheet and forgets to add them to the rate tab. His lookup is set to return 0 whenever there is no match. Why is that a poor choice on a sheet that produces invoices?

options.text: Zero pushes the peso column into text format, and the sheet's later totals then stop adding correctly
Zero is a valid rate for pro bono work, so the column can no longer be sorted into a sensible order
Zero adds silently into every total below it, so an unbilled client leaves no visible trace anywhere in the sheet
Zero has to be hunted down and typed over by hand on each affected row, which is slow on a long sheet

quiz.explanation: A wrong figure that stops you is cheap, and one that adds up neatly is not. Returning something unsummable, such as the text NO RATE, breaks the total and sends you looking, so the gap is found before an invoice goes out rather than after. A returned zero changes no formatting, and the cost is not the typing: it is that nothing ever sends you looking. It simply disappears into the sum.

quiz.prompt: Marilou leaves the delivery charge column blank on the rows where she collected the parts herself. AVERAGE over that column returns a figure noticeably higher than she expected across the month. What is the honest way to handle it?

options.text: Fill each blank with a zero, so the column holds a value on every row and the average uses them all
Decide whether a blank here means a zero charge or no delivery, then average only the rows that apply
Leave it exactly as it is, since AVERAGE skips blanks and the figure it returned is the charge per purchase
Average the delivery charge column across the whole year instead, so one month's mix stops distorting it

quiz.explanation: AVERAGE ignores blanks, so what came back is the average charge across delivered orders. That is a real answer to a different question. Filling in zeros answers a charge-per-purchase question, which may well be the one she wants, but only once she has decided which question she is asking and written that decision down. Widening the window to a year averages a different set of months and still never says what a blank in the column means.

quiz.prompt: Rhea's monthly summary has customers down the side and weeks across the top, with a total row and a total column. Adding up the row totals gives one figure. Adding up the column totals gives a figure a few hundred pesos apart. What does that gap tell her?

options.text: The two directions round differently, and a gap of this size is normal in peso work of this kind
One of the two total formulas covers a range that is missing a row or a column of the actual data
The sheet is due a recalculation, because a total built out of other totals refreshes on a delay
A customer's weekly figures went in as text, which the row totals leave out and the column totals include

quiz.explanation: The same numbers added in two directions have to agree, which is what makes cross-footing worth the minute it takes. A disagreement means a range does not cover what you think it covers, and comparing the two totals points you at the row or column that was missed. Rounding cannot produce a gap of hundreds of pesos, and text figures would be skipped in both directions equally rather than in only one.
