lessons.title: Cleaning an export without losing it
lessons.content_mdx:
# Cleaning an export without losing it

Marissa runs the back office for a small skincare seller in Bacolod. Once a month she downloads the shop's sales export and turns it into a figure the owner can act on. The file that arrives has never once been ready to use.

The first row is the shop's name, not a header. The real headers are spread over two rows, so "Order" sits above "Date" and neither is a column name on its own. Customer names carry trailing spaces you cannot see. Amounts came through as text with a peso sign and a comma typed inside the cell, so nothing sums. Four rows in the middle look repeated, and she does not yet know whether that is a fault in the export or two customers who each bought twice that afternoon.

None of that means the export is bad. Cleaning is the work.

## Copy the raw sheet before you touch anything

Chapter 1 set the three layers up: raw, working, output. This is the month they earn their keep.

Duplicate the downloaded tab. Call one of them raw, with the download date in the name, and do every fix on the copy.

This is not tidiness. A month later the owner asks why the sheet says one figure and the dashboard says another. If Marissa cleaned in place, she cannot answer, because the version she would need to compare against no longer exists. Downloading again does not rescue her: the shop has taken orders since, so the new file is a different file, and it still does not tell her what she changed.

## Keep a fix log

One line per change, on a tab of its own: what was wrong, what you did, how many rows it touched, and the date. It reads like this.

- Trailing spaces in Customer, trimmed, 96 rows, 14 August.
- Amounts held as text with peso signs and commas, symbols stripped and the column converted to numbers, whole column, 14 August.
- Three spellings of Perez Beauty Bar standardised to one, 31 rows, 14 August.

The log costs a few minutes. It is the only thing that later lets anyone, including you, tell a fix from a mistake.

## Count the rows before and after

Write down the row count of the raw copy. Write it down again when you finish. If the two numbers differ, your log has to account for the difference, line by line, and the arithmetic has to work.

A cleaned sheet with fewer rows than the export and no explanation is not clean. It is smaller, and nobody can say what left it.

## The techniques, by what they do

Every spreadsheet tool can do these. What each one is called, and where it sits in the menus, differs between tools, versions and language settings, so look for the behaviour in the tool in front of you rather than a name you read somewhere.

- **Trimming** strips spaces from the ends of a text value. Do it before you compare or group anything, because a name with a trailing space is a different name to a formula.
- **Splitting a column** pulls "Ilagan / website copy" into a client column and a project column, so you can group by either.
- **Find and replace** turns several spellings into one. Run one spelling at a time and read the count of replacements it reports, because a careless replace edits things you never looked at.
- **Sorting** pushes the strangest values to the top and the bottom. A negative amount, a date in the wrong year and an empty customer all surface in seconds.
- **Filtering** lets you see one problem at a time. Filter to blank amounts, fix those, clear the filter, move to the next problem.

Work one breakage at a time across the whole column, not one row at a time down the sheet. Row by row is where a fix log quietly dies.

## Decide what a duplicate is before you delete one

Repeated rows are where a cleaner does real damage. Two rows carrying the same customer, the same date and the same amount can be one sale imported twice, or a customer who bought the same item twice that afternoon. The sheet cannot tell you which.

So write the rule first, for this file. In a sales export that carries a transaction reference, a duplicate is two rows sharing that reference, and nothing weaker counts. In a client hours sheet with no reference at all, the honest move is to ask the person who kept it before you touch anything.

Then mark rather than delete. Add a column, flag the suspects, and exclude the flagged rows from your totals with a condition. A deletion is a decision nobody can inspect afterwards. A flag is one they can.

Marissa's file ends as three tabs: raw, working, and the fix log. When somebody challenges her figure, she can walk it back to the row, and back to the file the row arrived in.

## Do this now

Duplicate the last export you were sent, date the copy, and open a fix log tab with one line on it: the row count you started with, and today's date.

lessons.title: A pivot answers one question
lessons.content_mdx:
# A pivot answers one question

Dennis does admin support for three clients in Davao and keeps a client hours sheet: one row per block of work, carrying the date, the client, the project, the hours and who did them. It has grown past a thousand rows. Somebody asks how much time went to Sandoval Dental in July.

He can filter and read the total off the bottom. He does that once. Then he does it for August, then for the other two clients, then again when the question turns into hours by project. That is the point where a pivot earns its place.

## Write the question as a sentence first

Before touching anything, write it out: "Hours by client by month, for the first half of the year."

Then read your own sentence back. Hours is the thing being added up. Client and month are what the rows get grouped by. The half year is a filter. Every pivot you will ever build is those three parts, and the sentence is where you find them.

Questions that work in that shape: sales by product by week. Expenses by category for one client. Hours by staff member by month.

A request that fails the test: "a summary of the sheet." That is not a question, and no pivot answers it.

## What a pivot is doing

Grouping rows, then adding up a column. That is all.

Every row whose client is Sandoval Dental and whose date falls in July goes into one bucket, and the hours in that bucket are added. The answer is computed from the rows rather than typed by you, so when a row is corrected or a week is added, the summary moves with it. That is the difference between a pivot and a total you typed into a cell. One of them is still true next month.

Rows and columns are what you group by. Values are what you add up. If you catch yourself dragging hours into the rows, the question in your head was not the one you wrote down.

## One question, one pivot

The temptation is to keep adding. Client down the side, month across the top, then project as a second grouping, then a filter for one staff member, and now nobody can say what the table shows, including you.

Build a second pivot instead. They cost nothing. Two clean summaries that each answer one written sentence beat one summary that answers a question nobody asked.

## Check it against the source

A pivot looks authoritative in a way a typed total never does. Check it anyway, every time, once.

Total the source column plainly, with nothing grouped and no filter, across exactly the range the pivot reads. Set that beside the pivot's grand total. They should agree to the centavo.

When they do not, look at the data before you look at the pivot. The usual causes are all data:

- Some values in the column are text rather than numbers, so they were skipped and counted as nothing.
- The pivot's range stops short of the rows somebody added last week.
- Blanks in the grouping column sent rows into a group with no name, which is easy to miss at the bottom of a long table.

Each of those is a data problem wearing a pivot's clothes. Fix it in the working sheet, then refresh.

And a match is not a full pass. It proves the pivot read the column you pointed it at. It does not prove the rows belong to the period you meant, so check the earliest and latest dates inside your range as well. Dennis's July figure once came out high because a row dated last July sat inside the range, and both totals agreed with each other perfectly.

## A pivot over dirty data is worse than no pivot

This is why the cleaning comes first.

If Bautista Wellness appears three ways in the client column, the pivot does not warn you. It reports three clients, each with a tidy total, in the same clean type as everything else. Dennis sends the owner a summary showing a client at a fraction of the hours she actually bought, and nothing on the page looks wrong.

The pivot did its job. It grouped what was in front of it. Grouping is only as good as the spelling underneath it, and the polish hides the mess rather than revealing it.

So before you group anything, sort the client column and read the distinct names. Sort the category column and read those. It takes a minute, and it is the minute that keeps the summary honest.

## Do this now

Take a sheet you already keep and write the pivot question as one sentence, naming what gets added up, what it gets grouped by, and what the filter is. If the sentence will not come out, you have found the problem before you built anything.

lessons.title: One chart, one question
lessons.content_mdx:
# One chart, one question

Kaye keeps the expense tracker for a small logistics outfit in Cebu. The owner asked for "a chart of our expenses" for the monthly meeting. She built one: twelve months, six categories stacked, a second line for headcount, all in the company colours.

Nobody in the meeting could say what it showed. It was not a badly drawn chart. It was several charts pretending to be one.

## The question comes first, then the chart

Decide what single sentence the picture has to answer, and write that sentence down. Then choose the shape that answers it.

Three shapes cover the questions an operations sheet gets asked.

**Change over time.** "Did fuel spend go up between January and June?" Time along the bottom, the measure up the side, one line or one column series carrying it. One measure, unless a second genuinely belongs beside it.

**Comparison between categories.** "Which client took the most hours last month?" Bars, sorted from largest to smallest, labels readable without turning your head. The sorting is what makes the comparison instant.

**Share of a whole.** "How much of the spend is fuel?" This is the one that pulls everybody towards a pie. A pie with three slices says less than a two-row table, and a pie with nine slices says nothing at all. Write the shares as a short table with the total underneath, and the reader gets the answer and the underlying figures in one look.

## A chart carrying two questions answers neither

Kaye's chart tried to show the category mix, the movement across the year, and a relationship with headcount. Any one of those is a chart. The three together is a shape the reader has to decode instead of read.

Split it. Fuel by month as a line. The category mix for the latest month as a short table. If the headcount relationship matters, that is a third picture, and it is probably a sentence.

## Labels are not decoration

A chart that leaves the room without labels becomes whatever the reader assumes it is.

Anything you hand over carries four things: what the vertical axis measures and in what units, what the horizontal axis is, a title that states the question the chart answers, and the period covered. "Fuel spend by month, pesos, January to June" is a title. "Expenses" is not.

If the axis is rounded to thousands, say so on the axis. A reader who takes 40 to mean forty pesos rather than forty thousand is not being careless. Nobody told them.

## What a chart owes a client report

Beside the chart, in small type, put three things: the sheet it came from, the date range of the data, and the date you made it.

Three months from now that image will be sitting in an email thread with no file attached to it. Whoever opens it needs to see that it covers January to June and was built in July, or they will read it as current and act on it. This is the same discipline as a reference number on a row. A figure that cannot be walked back to the sheet behind it is a figure you will end up defending from memory.

## Cut anything that carries no information

Gradients, drop shadows, three-dimensional depth, a photo behind the bars, gridlines at every small step, a legend for a single series. Each one costs the reader time and returns nothing.

Ask it of every element on the chart: if I removed this, would the reader lose an answer? If not, remove it.

## When a table beats any chart

Two numbers with a comparison between them do not need a picture. "Fuel in January, ₱48,000. Fuel in June, ₱61,000." Those are figures invented for this example, and a chart of two values is decoration wrapped around a sentence.

Exact figures that the reader will copy into something else belong in a table too. A chart is for shape: rising, falling, this bar taller than the rest, this month unlike the others. When the reader needs the number itself, hand them the number.

Kaye rebuilt hers as one line chart with a labelled axis and a four-row table, both marked with the source sheet and the date range. The meeting made the decision it had been circling for a month, and when the owner asked where a figure came from, Kaye could answer in one sentence.

## Do this now

Open the last chart you sent anybody. Write down the one question it was meant to answer, then check whether the title says that question and whether the axis says its units. Fix whichever of the two is missing.

quiz.prompt: Marissa cleaned her client's sales export on the downloaded tab itself, then sent the owner a monthly total. Three weeks later the owner says the figure does not match the shop dashboard. Where does that leave Marissa?

options.text: In reasonable shape, since the file is still open and she can step back through every edit she made.
Rebuilding formulas, since they now read edited cells and have to be redone before she can compare.
Slightly delayed, because downloading the export again today settles the difference in minutes.
With no way to show what the export said on arrival, and no record of which fix moved the total.

quiz.explanation: Cleaning in place destroys the two things a challenged figure needs: the untouched arrival copy, and a log of what changed. Undo does not survive a closed file and is not a record anybody else can read. Downloading again gives her a different file, because the shop has taken orders since. Broken formulas would be the smaller problem, and are not what the owner is asking about.

quiz.prompt: Dennis hands a colleague a cleaned copy of a sales export. The raw file had 1,412 rows and the cleaned sheet has 1,388. There is no fix log anywhere in the file. What should the colleague do?

options.text: Work from the cleaned sheet, since a small number of dropped rows will not move a monthly total.
Ask Dennis to account for the missing rows, and rebuild from the raw copy if he cannot say why.
Compare the two grand totals, and treat a match as proof that nothing important was removed.
Delete the cleaned sheet and clean the raw copy again, so only his own edits are in the file.

quiz.explanation: A row count that fell with nothing explaining it is the whole reason a fix log exists. Ask first, because Dennis may have a good reason he simply did not write down. Cleaning again immediately throws away work that may be correct and still does not say what happened. Matching totals prove only that the removed rows summed to nothing, which is what a deleted blank looks like and also what a deleted unpaid order looks like.

quiz.prompt: An export of Marissa's sales has rows that look repeated. She deletes every row sharing a customer, a date and an amount with another row. The owner later finds two genuine same-day purchases missing. What should she have done?

options.text: Written down what counts as a duplicate in this file first, then flagged the suspects rather than deleting them.
Sorted by customer first, and deleted only the repeats that ended up sitting next to each other.
Checked the row count before and after, which would have shown her the deletion had gone too far.
Deleted the repeats as she did, but kept a copy of the removed rows on a separate tab of the file.

quiz.explanation: Same customer, same day, same amount is not a duplicate. It is a customer who bought twice. In a file carrying a transaction reference, a duplicate is two rows sharing that reference, and nothing weaker counts. Flagging keeps the decision visible and reversible. Sorting makes repeats adjacent, it does not make them duplicates. A row count says how many rows left, never which ones deserved to. Keeping the removed rows elsewhere is better than nothing but still applies the wrong rule.

quiz.prompt: Dennis's pivot of hours by client shows Bautista Wellness three times, each with its own total, because the client column holds three spellings. The sheet carries no client code. What is the fix?

options.text: Standardise the spelling in the working sheet, log the change with a row count, then refresh the pivot.
Group the three rows inside the pivot itself, which leaves the source exactly as the export sent it.
Add the three totals together in the report, with a note under the table saying they are one client.
Filter the pivot to the spelling used in the client's own contract, since that is the version that is correct.

quiz.explanation: The pivot is reporting what is in the column, so the column is what has to change, on the working copy, with the row count logged. Adding the totals by hand works once and breaks the moment anyone refreshes or a fourth spelling arrives. Grouping inside the pivot hides the problem and leaves every other summary built on that column wrong. Filtering to one spelling drops the hours recorded under the other two, which is the client's billable time going missing.

quiz.prompt: Kaye's pivot of expenses by category comes back with a grand total lower than a plain total of the same amount column over the same rows. Where does she look first?

options.text: At the pivot setup, since a grand total disagreeing with the column means it adds the wrong field.
At the rounding, since a pivot rounds each group to the peso before adding them into a grand total.
At the data, for amounts sitting as text and for rows outside the range the pivot reads.
At neither yet, since a plain total counts blank rows the pivot has correctly left out of its groups.

quiz.explanation: A gap of this shape is a data problem wearing a pivot's clothes. The two usual causes are amounts stored as text, which get skipped and counted as nothing, and a range that stops short of rows somebody added later. Fix them in the working sheet and refresh. A pivot adding the wrong field would give a total unrelated to the column rather than one slightly under it. Pivots do not silently round groups, and a blank adds nothing to a plain total either.

quiz.prompt: Dennis checks his pivot's grand total against a plain total of the hours column and they agree exactly. The July figure he is about to send is still too high. What did that match fail to prove?

options.text: That the hours column holds no blanks, since a blank would have pulled the two totals apart.
That every session was logged in decimal hours, since 1h 45m in a cell would add on one side only.
That the pivot's range reaches the last row, since a range stopping short would leave its total lower.
That every row in the range belongs to July, which only a look at the earliest and latest dates shows.

quiz.explanation: Both totals read the same rows, so both happily include a row dated last July if one is sitting in the range. The reconciliation checks the adding, not the selecting, so read the earliest and latest date inside the range before you trust the period. Blanks and text values are skipped on both sides equally, so neither pulls the two figures apart, and both would push a figure down rather than up. A range that stops short of the data is one of the few faults the match does catch, because the two totals would then differ.

quiz.prompt: Kaye is about to email a client a column chart titled Expenses. The vertical axis runs to 60 with no units on it, and the bottom axis reads Jan to Jun. What has to change before it goes?

options.text: Units on the axis and the source noted beside it, since the title and the month labels already say what it covers.
A title stating the question, units on the vertical axis, and the period and source written beside it.
Only the title, since a client reading their own expense chart can infer the units from the scale used.
Nothing on the chart, as long as the covering email states the period, the source and the units.

quiz.explanation: An axis running to 60 could be pesos, thousands of pesos or deliveries, and a reader who guesses wrong is not being careless. Expenses is a subject, not a question, so the title has to say what the chart answers. The email is the weakest place to carry any of it, because the image gets forwarded, screenshotted and reopened months later with no email attached to it. Units and a source still leave a chart titled Expenses, which names a subject rather than the question it answers.

quiz.prompt: The owner asks Kaye two things for one slide: whether fuel spend is rising, and which expense category takes the largest share of the month. What should she put on the slide?

options.text: One stacked column chart by month, which carries the movement and the category mix in a single picture.
One pie of the category shares, with a line under it saying which way fuel has moved since January.
A line of fuel by month, and a short table of category shares beside it, each under its own heading.
One combined chart with fuel drawn as a line and the category totals as columns on a second axis.

quiz.explanation: Two questions, so two pictures, each labelled with the question it answers. A share of a whole reads better as a short table than as a pie, because the reader gets the ranking and the actual figures at once. A stacked column asks the reader to compare segment heights that do not share a baseline, which is how a rising category can look flat. A second axis lets two unrelated measures be scaled until they appear related, and the reader has no way to tell.

modules.title: AI on the sheet, and the checking it cannot do
modules.description: AI is genuinely useful for writing and explaining formulas and genuinely unreliable as a calculator. This chapter draws that line, sets the checks that catch a wrong figure before it leaves your hands, and says what must never be pasted into a chat box at all. It covers a general chat assistant used from outside the sheet, by design: the AI features now built into individual spreadsheet products change too often for a course to describe safely, so they are left to each tool's own current documentation rather than covered, or promised, here.

lessons.title: Ask for the formula, not the answer
lessons.content_mdx:
# Ask for the formula, not the answer

Two requests, one minute apart, on the same sheet.

**Request one.** Marivic copies 240 rows out of her client hours sheet, pastes them into a chat window and types: "total the Hours column." A number comes back in seconds, tidily formatted, inside a confident sentence.

**Request two.** She types instead: "I am in Google Sheets. One row is one work session. Column D is Hours, stored as a plain number. Data runs from row 2 to row 241 and I add rows every week. Give me a formula that totals Hours for client CL-004 only, where the client code sits in column B. Explain each part."

The second request hands her something she can test on rows whose answer she already knows. The first hands her something she can only believe.

That is the move this chapter rests on. Ask for the thing that computes, never for the thing that resembles a computation.

## Why the pasted column is the wrong request

A chat reply is text. Some tools do run real code on what you paste and some only write the sentence a total would appear in, and which one you are talking to is not something the reply tells you. Even when the arithmetic was genuinely done, nothing in the reply says so, and nobody opening your sheet next month can see where the figure came from.

The failure is quiet, which is what makes it dangerous. A total that missed four rows does not come back flagged. It arrives with two decimal places and a confident sentence around it.

The sheet is the calculator. It already holds the data, it adds the same way every time, and when three more sessions go in next week the formula picks them up while a pasted answer stays frozen at the moment you pasted.

## What a formula request has to carry

You already know how to write a brief. These are the parts specific to a sheet.

**Which tool you are in.** Excel and Google Sheets do not offer the same functions, and what exists differs between versions of the same product. Say which one you are in, and be ready to be handed a function your copy does not have. When that happens, ask for a version built from older, plainer functions.

**What one row represents.** One sale, one expense, one session. Everything the formula does downstream depends on this and it is the part people leave out.

**The exact headers and where they sit.** Not "the amount column". "Column F, header Amount, plain number, no currency typed in the cell."

**The range, and whether it grows.** A formula written for rows 2 to 241 quietly ignores row 242.

**What should happen at the edges.** No match found. A blank cell. Text sitting where a number should be. If you do not say, the model decides for you, and it picks something, often a zero standing in for "I do not know", and it does not tell you it chose.

## Ask for three things in one reply

**The formula.**

**An explanation of each part.** Not "this sums by client." Which argument is the range, which is the condition, what the pinning does. If you cannot read a formula back as a sentence, you cannot maintain it and you cannot answer for it.

**What would break it.** Ask straight out: "what would make this return a wrong number rather than an error?" The answers worth having are specific. A client code with a trailing space. A row pasted below the range. Hours stored as text.

## The formula somebody else left behind

The VA before you has gone. You open her sales log and column K holds ninety characters of nested functions, and the figure it produces goes to a client every month.

Do not edit it. Paste it, say which tool you are in, describe what the sheet holds, and ask what it does step by step and what it assumes about the data. Then check that explanation against two rows you can work out yourself.

This is the safest thing AI does on a spreadsheet: reading something that already exists back to you in words. Even a partly wrong explanation gives you named parts to test instead of a wall of brackets, and once you can say what the formula does, you can decide whether it stays.

## The one thing not to do

Do not use a chat as a calculator. Not for a total, not for a percentage, not for "roughly how much is this."

And if you have already pasted a column and asked for the total, the fix is not to ask the model to check its work. That produces a second confident paragraph, not a second calculation. Put the numbers back in the sheet and total them where the adding happens.

## Do this now

Write the request, and do not send it yet. Name the tool you are in, say what one row is, list the headers with their column letters, give the range, and say what should happen at a blank. Read it back and see how much of it you had to go and look up.

lessons.title: Checking what looks right
lessons.content_mdx:
# Checking what looks right

A wrong figure in a spreadsheet does not look wrong. It sits in the same font, in the same column, with the same two decimal places as the correct figure beside it. The screen is never going to tell you. The only thing that catches it is a check you decided to run.

Here is the order to run them in. The whole sequence takes a few minutes, and it is the difference between a number you sent and a number you can defend.

## 1. Test it where you already know the answer

Before a new formula is trusted anywhere, point it at rows whose answer you already hold. If you know client CL-004 had four sessions in July, run the formula for CL-004 in July. If it says three, you have learned that now instead of after the invoice went out.

Choose your test rows on purpose. One ordinary row. One at the edge of the range, the first of the month or the last row of data. One awkward row: a blank, a zero, a cancelled session. A formula that survives the awkward row is worth more than one that sailed through five easy ones.

## 2. Recompute a row by hand

Paper, phone calculator, whatever is nearest. Take one row, work the arithmetic yourself, compare.

This is the same check chapter 2 asked for, and it is here for the same reason: it is the one step in the whole process where a human being does the sum. Its partner from that chapter belongs here too. Add the row totals down the side, add the column totals across the bottom, and see whether the two agree. When they do not, something in the middle is being counted twice or not counted at all.

Two checks, both cheap. Between them they catch the errors that actually reach a client.

## 3. Reconcile against the source

Your formula produced a figure for one client. Now total the whole Amount column plainly, with no conditions, and produce the same figure for every other client. Do the parts add up to the whole?

When they do not, the cause is usually the data rather than the formula. A row carrying a client code nobody assigned. An amount stored as text, which adds as nothing. Four spellings of one client where you expected one. That is a chapter 3 problem arriving late, and far better found here than in front of the client.

## 4. Count the rows

Before a change, write down how many rows the sheet has. After the change, count again. If the number moved and you did not mean it to, stop and find out why.

This matters when a formula arrives with a helpful suggestion attached: remove the duplicates first, filter out the blanks, delete the junk at the bottom. Every one of those is a row count event, and a row that vanishes quietly is the hardest thing on this list to notice later.

## 5. Bounds checks

Ask three questions of the finished column. The answer should be obvious every time.

**Can this be negative?** Hours worked cannot be. If a negative appears, a subtraction is running backwards or a refund has landed in a column that does not expect one.

**Can a part be larger than its whole?** One client's hours cannot exceed total hours. One category cannot exceed the month.

**Does every date fall inside the period?** A June summary containing a May date means the range is wrong, or the date column is part text and the sort quietly lied to you.

## The formula you cannot read

This one overrides the others. If you cannot say in ordinary words what a formula does, do not keep it, however well it behaves on the rows you tested.

"It adds column F wherever column B matches the client code in this row, and shows a blank when there is no match" is readable. Ninety characters of brackets you accepted because the total looked about right is not. The rows you tested are not the rows that will break it, and on the day it breaks the number will still look exactly like a number.

If the explanation you were handed is too dense to say out loud, ask for it again in plainer parts, or split the formula across two columns so each step is visible. A longer sheet you understand beats a clever one you do not.

## Why the chapter exists at all

A wrong figure does not stay in the sheet.

It becomes the amount on a client's invoice, and you are the one asking for the difference back. It becomes a line in somebody's pay, which is a conversation with a person who was counting on that number. It becomes part of the record behind a filing, where the correction costs somebody's paid time and the sheet is what everyone opens first.

None of that is dramatic. It is simply expensive, and all of it is prevented by the few minutes above.

## Do this now

Take a formula already sitting in a sheet you keep and run check 2 on it. One row, worked out by hand, and not the first one.

lessons.title: What goes in the box
lessons.content_mdx:
# What goes in the box

Think about what is actually sitting in the sheets you work on. A client hours sheet carries names and rates. An order export carries mobile numbers and delivery addresses. A payroll tab carries TINs, bank account numbers and what every person in that company earns.

A spreadsheet is often the densest personal data anybody hands you all year, and a chat window has no idea what is in it.

## The general rule is not new

AI Essentials for Work holds the full list of what never goes into a chatbot, and it applies here with nothing added: government ID numbers, bank details, other people's personal data, anything unreleased. Read it if you have not. Pasting is sending to an outside company, and deleting the chat afterwards does not un-send anything.

What this lesson adds is the spreadsheet move, because a spreadsheet question is unusually easy to ask without the data.

## Ask about the shape, not the contents

A formula does not need anybody's name. It needs the layout.

So build a fake sheet. Five rows is plenty. Same headers, same column order, same data types, invented contents.

```
Client   | Date       | Hours | Rate | Amount
Client A | 2026-03-02 | 3     | 500  | 1500
Client A | 2026-03-04 | 2.5   | 500  | 1250
Client B | 2026-03-04 | 4     | 650  | 2600
Client B | 2026-03-09 |       | 650  |
Client A | 2026-03-11 | 1     | 500  | 500
```

Those rates are invented so the example has something in the cells. Yours will look nothing like them, and that is the point.

Then ask: "Column C is Hours as a number, column D is a rate, one row is one session, and some sessions have a blank in Hours because the timesheet was not filled in. In Google Sheets, write me a formula that totals Amount for Client A in March, and tell me what it does with the blank."

You get the same formula you would have got by uploading the real file, because it is the same question. What you did not do is hand a stranger twenty-two people's pay.

Put the awkward rows in on purpose. One blank. One client code with a trailing space. One row that should be excluded. Those are the rows a formula has to survive, and inventing them takes less time than describing them.

## The client's file is not yours to upload

Even when nothing in it looks sensitive, you hold that file to do a job, not to pass it on. Your service agreement may say so directly, in a confidentiality clause you signed at onboarding and have not opened since. Go and read the clause before you decide, not afterwards.

If you genuinely cannot reduce a question to a shape, ask the client in writing and keep the reply. Being the person who asked first is a far better position than being the person asked about it later.

## The privacy obligation sits on you

If you hold information that describes other people, obligations follow, and they do not disappear because you work alone from a bedroom. Which of them reach you depends on what you hold and why. What applies to your situation, and what you have to do about it, is a question for the National Privacy Commission, whose guidance is published and free to read.

Do not ask a chatbot this. It is exactly the category where a tidy, confident, wrong answer is most likely and most expensive, and where the real answer is a search away at the source.

## The same rule on the record side

Your sheet is not the filing. It supports the filing.

Everything in this course points one way: keep records solid enough that when something has to be filed, or a bookkeeper asks a question, or a client queries an amount, the answer is a figure you can walk back to the document behind it. What must be filed, on which form, by when and by whom is not in this course and is not in a chat window either. That is bir.gov.ph, your RDO, or a bookkeeper you pay. Those rules change, and nobody tells the model when they do.

## Where the line sits

A chat reply containing a total is text that resembles a total. It came out of a system built to write convincing sentences. A spreadsheet is a system built to add. Keep each doing the thing it is for.

Ask the chat for instructions you can test. Run them in the sheet. Check the result against rows you already know. Then put your name on the figure, and not before.

The formula can be drafted by anyone. The number is yours.

## Do this now

Build the fake sheet before you need it. Five rows, the same headers and column order as the file you actually work on, invented contents, one blank and one code with a trailing space. Keep it in a file of its own so the next question costs you nothing.

quiz.prompt: Grace does admin for a construction supplier in Iloilo. The owner sends her the payroll tab: twenty-two employees, full names, mobile numbers, TINs, bank account numbers and monthly pay. She needs a formula for net pay after deductions, and she is about to paste the tab into a chat window. What should she do instead?

options.text: Ask using five invented rows carrying the same headers, then run the returned formula on the real tab herself.
Ask the owner for written permission first, then paste the whole tab so the formula fits the real columns.
Skip the formula and work the twenty-two net pay figures out by hand, since asking at all risks the file leaving her machine.
Screenshot the payroll tab and attach the image instead, since an image is not a file the tool can keep.

quiz.explanation: A formula needs the layout, not the contents: which column holds what, what one row means, and what to do at the edges. Five invented rows carry all of that and nobody's salary. A screenshot sends the same twenty-two people's pay, in a picture rather than a file. Working every figure out by hand throws away help she could have had safely and leaves nothing that still works next month. Permission from the owner is worth having but is a separate question from whether the data has to leave at all. Philippine privacy obligations sit on whoever holds other people's personal information, and the National Privacy Commission is where you check what applies to you.

quiz.prompt: Ronnel keeps the expense tracker for a small printing shop in Cagayan de Oro. He asks a chatbot when the shop's next quarterly return is due and which form to use. The answer arrives at once, with a specific date, a form number and no hedging at all. What should he do with it?

options.text: Check it against a bookkeeping blog that lists this year's deadlines, and use the date once the two agree.
Ask the same question again in a fresh chat and accept the answer once the two replies agree with each other.
Treat it as unconfirmed, check the BIR's own site or his RDO, and set the calendar entry from what he finds.
Plan the month around it now and confirm it nearer the time, since the date only matters on the day itself.

quiz.explanation: A confident date is not a checked date, two chats agreeing is one habit repeated rather than a second source, and a blog is somebody's summary of the rule, sometimes accurate and sometimes a year out of date. Deadlines, form numbers and thresholds get changed by legislation and by new issuances, so the current version lives at the source: bir.gov.ph, his RDO, or a bookkeeper he pays. His sheet supports the filing. It does not decide the rule.

quiz.prompt: Aileen holds a client's order file: six hundred rows of customer names, mobile numbers, addresses and order totals. Her service agreement has a confidentiality clause she signed at onboarding and has not read since. She wants help writing a lookup, and plans to upload the file and delete the chat afterwards. What is the sound move?

options.text: Upload it and delete the chat afterwards, since nothing of the client's is left behind once it is gone.
Re-read that clause and ask the client in writing, and meanwhile use five invented rows for the formula.
Upload it with the name column removed, since order numbers and amounts do not identify anybody by themselves.
Type twenty of the real rows into the chat by hand, since typing them is not the same as uploading the file.

quiz.explanation: Deleting a chat does not un-send it, because the file left her machine the moment it was uploaded. Typing the rows in by hand sends exactly the same customer details, one keystroke at a time. A mobile number and an address identify a person on their own, so dropping the name column changes little. The clause she signed may already answer this, which is why it gets read before the decision rather than after one. Meanwhile the lookup can be written against five invented rows with the same headers and run on the real file at her end.

quiz.prompt: Marlon inherits a sales log. Column K holds ninety characters of nested functions and produces the commission figure emailed to the client every month. Nobody left on the team can say what it does. What should he do first?

options.text: Paste it into a chat, ask for a shorter formula that returns the same number, and swap the new one in.
Ask AI what it does step by step, then test that against three rows he can work out himself.
Replace it with a hand total each month until somebody who understands the original becomes available.
Leave it and keep sending the figure, since it has produced a sensible number every month so far.

quiz.explanation: Reading an existing formula back to you in words is the safest thing AI does on a spreadsheet, and even a partly wrong explanation gives him named parts to test instead of a wall of brackets. Asking for a shorter formula that returns the same number swaps one thing he cannot read for another, on the cell that produces a client's figure. Sending a figure nobody understands is the situation he is trying to get out of, and totalling it by hand every month is the running cost of never finding out. Testing the explanation against rows he can work out himself is what turns it into evidence.

quiz.prompt: Jhoanna asked for a formula and got one that returns the right total on every row she has checked. There is one part of it she cannot explain, and she does not want to look slow by asking again. The figure it produces goes straight into a monthly invoice. What should she do?

options.text: Total the invoice by hand alongside it each month, so the sheet is only ever a cross-check on her figure.
Rewrite it herself from what she thinks it should compute, and use her version once the totals agree.
Test it against twenty more rows, and treat twenty clean passes as enough to keep a formula she cannot read.
Get the part she cannot explain rewritten in plainer terms, and keep only a formula she can say out loud.

quiz.explanation: Working on the rows you tested is exactly what a wrong formula also does, and the rows nobody tested are the ones that eventually pay somebody. Twenty more clean passes change nothing about that, because she still cannot say what the formula does at an edge she has not met. Rewriting it from what she thinks it should do leaves her holding two figures and no way to choose between them. Recomputing by hand every month is the running cost of keeping something unreadable. A figure that leaves your hands is one you have to be able to explain, so the formula behind it has to be one you can say in words.

quiz.prompt: Bea pastes a hundred and eighty expense amounts into a chat window and asks for the total. Back comes a figure to two decimal places, inside a neat sentence. It is going into the month's summary for the client. What should she do?

options.text: Total the column in the sheet instead, since the sheet is the only place the addition actually happens.
Ask the chat to check its own total, and use the figure once the second answer matches the first one.
Add ten of the rows herself, and take the chat's figure if her ten land inside the range she expected.
Add all hundred and eighty on a calculator and send her own figure, since a person adding them is safest.

quiz.explanation: A chat reply is text shaped like a total. It can land on the right figure, and nothing in the reply tells you whether this was one of those times. Asking it to check itself produces a second confident paragraph, not a second calculation. Ten rows checked says nothing about the other hundred and seventy. Adding all hundred and eighty on a calculator is a real calculation and a poor one: it is slow, it is easy to slip a row, and it has to be done again from scratch next month. The sheet already holds the numbers, adds them the same way every time, and keeps working when more rows arrive.

quiz.prompt: Rico asked AI for a formula that averages hours per session for one client, got back a total divided by a count of rows, checked it against the three rows sitting at the top of the sheet, and sent the figure to the client. Hundreds of rows down, sessions with a blank in the Hours column are being counted as zero, and the average he sent was low. Which check would have caught it before it left?

options.text: Reading the formula back as a sentence, which would have named the rows it was quietly leaving out.
Asking the same tool to review its own formula and confirm it handles every case in the sheet.
Comparing the sheet's row count before and after, which would have flagged the rows that were skipped.
Testing it on rows chosen on purpose, including an awkward one: a blank, a zero, or a row at the edge of the range.

quiz.explanation: The rows at the top of a sheet are the rows the formula was built against, so they agree with it and prove nothing. Test rows get picked on purpose: one ordinary, one at the edge of the range, and one awkward, which here is the blank the formula had never met. Reading it back would have told him it divides by every row, and it still would not have shown him a blank he had never met in the rows he tested. A tool reviewing its own output gives a second confident paragraph, not a second test. And the row count never moved, because nothing was added or deleted.

quiz.prompt: Angel wants a formula that brings each client's hourly rate across from a Rates sheet into her hours sheet. Her request so far reads, in full: give me a lookup formula for Google Sheets. What is the most useful thing to add to it?

options.text: How many rows each sheet holds and how often she adds to them, since the range is what breaks a lookup.
Both sheets pasted in full, so the tool can see the real data and build the formula around what it finds.
What one row is, the headers and their column letters, and what to show when a code has no match at all.
A request for the newest lookup function, since a newer one handles more situations than an older one.

quiz.explanation: A lookup's behaviour depends on things only she can supply: what a row represents, where each header sits, and what should appear when a code has no matching row. Row counts and how fast a sheet grows matter for the range and answer none of those. Pasting both sheets sends client names and rates to an outside company for a question that only needed the layout. And a function being newer says nothing about whether her copy has it, which is why the tool you are in belongs in the request rather than a demand for the latest thing.

assignment.title: One sheet you can defend
assignment.brief_mdx:
Rebuild one real sheet. Pick a sales log, an expense tracker or a client hours sheet: one you actually keep, one you inherited, or one you could plausibly be handed tomorrow. Work it the way this course works it, then submit the write-up as text. No file uploads. Aim for roughly 800 to 1,000 words.

1. **The sheet's job.** One sentence on what the sheet is for. One sentence saying what one row represents.
2. **The columns.** Every column, with its type (date, number, text, category) and a one-line data dictionary entry saying what it holds. Say which columns you added or split out of a combined field, and why.
3. **What was wrong.** What was actually broken in the version you started from, or in the export you were handed: a tab per month, a totals row sitting inside the data, peso signs typed into the amount cells, one client spelled four ways, dates that will not sort, a note parked in the amount column. Name what you found, not a general list of what can go wrong.
4. **The fix log.** One line per change: what was wrong, what you did, how many rows it touched. Give the row count before and after, and account for any difference. If the count dropped, say what you deleted and how you decided it was a duplicate.
5. **Three formulas.** Paste each one as text. Under each, one plain sentence saying what it does, and one specific thing that would break it. Use a conditional total, a lookup, and one formula of your choice.
6. **One pivot.** Write the question as a sentence first. Then paste the summary as a small table. Then say how you checked its grand total against a plain total of the source column, and what you would have done if the two had not matched.
7. **One chart, in words.** No image needed. Give the question it answers, the chart type, why that type and not another, and the labels it carries: what the axis measures, the units, the period covered, the source sheet.
8. **One AI exchange.** Paste what you asked and what came back, verbatim. You are asking for a formula, not for an answer. Then give the check you ran on it: tested on rows where you already knew the answer, one row recomputed by hand, or the total reconciled against the source. Then name at least one thing the AI got wrong, or that you could not confirm.
9. **What you took out.** What you removed or replaced before pasting anything into an AI tool, and why.

Four things decide the mark as much as the content. Your raw data stays untouched, so say where the raw copy sits and confirm nothing was typed over it. Every figure you show has to be walkable back to a row, a formula or a document reference. No real client names, mobile numbers, addresses, tax identification numbers or bank details anywhere in the submission: use Client A, Client B and invented amounts, and say the amounts are invented. If your example needs a rate, use one you were given or one you invent and label as invented. Nothing here asks you to state what anyone charges, what a platform takes, or what any agency requires.
criteria: Part 1 states what one row represents, and the column list in part 2 matches that definition: every column carries a type and a one-line description, with amounts as plain numbers, dates stored as dates, and categories drawn from a short fixed list rather than free text
The fix log gives a row count before and after with any difference accounted for, and the submission says where the untouched raw copy sits. A sheet edited directly over the original fails
